$comment: The shared contract: the bounds one send is held to, in one authoritative place.
A change here is a change to every SDK. Each target reads this file from its own suite and
holds its own defaults against it, so a number edited here fails every target that still
carries the old one, rather than being corrected once per language by whoever remembers.
The first seven bound what this client does. The last four bound what the other end may cost
it: a server that is broken or hostile can otherwise stream a body, a head or a header of any
length into a caller's memory, and a client with no ceiling has no answer to that. They are
written here rather than per language so that two targets cannot bound different things.
The four are not interchangeable, and all four are applied. `max_head_bytes` is the only one
that bounds the memory a head can cost, because it bounds the total; a line count and a size
per line multiply, and 64 lines of 64 KiB is 4 MiB of head admitted by both. Those two earn
their place by refusing early, on the first line past the count or the first line too long,
before the whole head has been read. Aggregate for the ceiling, components to refuse sooner.
16384 is what Node enforces by default, and that is the reason for the number rather than a
round figure: it is the ceiling of the strictest runtime any target runs on, so every target
can apply it in library code. Anything above it is not implementable in TypeScript at all —
Node refuses a larger head before the SDK is consulted, and the only lever is a process flag,
`--max-http-header-size`, which no library may require of the application embedding it. Margin
is therefore taken downwards, never upwards. That same flag can reopen Node's ceiling, which
is why every target applies this bound itself instead of inheriting whatever its runtime does
— two clients trusting only their runtimes returned opposite verdicts on one 61560-byte head.
Every bound here is a safety ceiling, and conformance to it is shown by the refusal above it.
Acceptance just below is deliberately not required: whether a head of 16000 bytes is read is
a liveness property that the runtime settles before a client is reached, and Node's effective
ceiling sits slightly above the 16384 it advertises. A target should exercise a head well
under the bound and a head well over it, and leave the band around the bound untested — a
case built there reports the runtime of the day rather than the client.
Every value is a ceiling a caller may lower and, for the ones a policy exposes, may raise up
to the hard cap. `max_attempts_cap` is the one nothing may cross: a policy is configuration,
and configuration can be wrong.
